goal.what: Maintainers, people or AI agents, change what the code does and know that every behavior its specification asks for still holds, and whoever runs the code can fix a wrong input from outside.

critical_success_factors.what: The maintainer finds the one place where a change belongs.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each module say, where the maintainer first meets it, the one thing it alone decides?
necessary_conditions.why: A maintainer with one behavior to change should find the one module to open without reading the bodies. David Parnas's [information hiding](https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623) gives each module one decision that the specification leaves to the code, most of all one that's likely to change.

items.text: List the decisions that the specification leaves to the code.
Give each decision to one module.

Where a decision meets a problem that a known design pattern solves, such as Strategy or Adapter in [Design Patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Patterns), use the pattern by its name, since the name gives the maintainer the whole design at once. Use it only where a case of the specification needs it now, as N3 says.
Have the module state its decision in a few words where the maintainer meets it first, such as at its top. If the module can't state it briefly, split the module.

Take a behavior that the specification might change, and read only what the modules say they decide. Check that it points to one module. Where it doesn't, rewrite what the modules say, or move the decision.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each name that a module offers state everything a caller needs to call it without reading its body?
necessary_conditions.why: A caller who needn't read the body lets the body change behind the interface without breaking them. [Design by contract](https://www.eiffel.com/values/design-by-contract/introduction/), by Bertrand Meyer, states what a call expects, what it gives, and what stays true.

items.text: Choose the names that other modules may use, and mark every other name as internal.
Give each name the types it takes and gives, such as in its signature where the language allows.

Write beside each name, such as in a doc comment, what it gives, what comes back when there's nothing to give, what it expects of what it takes, what else it changes, and each way it refuses a correct call.
Leave out what the types already say.
Have someone who hasn't read the body write a call from the interface alone, and run the call. Where the call fails or they had to guess, add what was missing.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each behavior of the code trace to a case of its specification, which is what the architecture asks of its part?
necessary_conditions.why: Every behavior that no one asked for is code the maintainer must carry and keep working. [You Aren't Gonna Need It](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/Yagni.html) keeps only what the cases ask for now, in the form they ask for.

items.text: For each option, mode, and case that the code handles, name the case of the specification that asks for it. The specification is what the architecture asks of the part: the decisions its line gives the part, the rules of the principles, and each step of a sequence that the part takes or answers, with the data as the data model names it.
Remove what no case asks for.

critical_success_factors.what: The tests show whether every behavior still holds.

necessary_conditions.what: Do the tests pass in any order and on every run, on a fresh machine set up from the code's setup alone?
necessary_conditions.why: When a test fails, the cause should lie in the code, never in the machine or in the order of the tests. A [hermetic](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html) test holds everything it needs to set up, run, and clear its environment.

items.text: Have the code's setup name everything the code needs, with the versions it runs on.
Have each test set up and clear everything it uses.

For each real tool the tests run, such as git, find each thing it does on its own beyond the call, such as reading the machine's settings or starting maintenance in the background, and turn it off in the test's own settings, so that the tool does only what the test asks of it.
Set the code up on a clean machine or container, from the code's setup alone, and add to the setup each missing thing that the setup or the tests found, such as a runtime.
Run the tests several times, and in a shuffled order, and check that they pass on every run.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each case of the specification, its edges and refusals included, have one test whose name says the case?
necessary_conditions.why: A maintainer whose test fails should know which case it breaks. [Test-driven development](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html) writes the tests from the specification's cases before the code.

items.text: Take the unit cases that the architecture's test cases hold for the part, each naming the integration case it supports, as [the architecture best practice](../architecture/best-practice.md) writes them before any code. These cases are the specification, so a case that no test names isn't in it.

Where the code needs a case that they don't hold, such as for a module inside the part, design it before its code as a test's name and its Given, When, and Then, the usual one, each edge, and each refusal, naming the case one level up that it supports. Take a case that names none back to the architecture, since it tests what no element asks for.
Write one test for each case, named for the behavior it checks. If the name needs `and`, split the test.

Write each test so that its reader grasps the situation, the action, and what must be so, such as in the three parts [Given, When, and Then](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GivenWhenThen.html), with each expected value taken from the specification, not from what the code gives.

Keep each test readable on its own, with the values that its case turns on in its own body, and put in one helper only setup that many tests share, such as building the object under test, since Software Engineering at Google advises that [unit tests](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch12.html) be descriptive and meaningful rather than free of repetition.
Keep loops and branches out of a test, as the same source advises.
Give each failure a message that names the case, as the same source advises.
Run each test before you write its code, and see it fail.
Read the tests as a maintainer whose test failed would, and check that each test checks one case, that its name says the case, and that it names the case one level up that it supports.

necessary_conditions.what: Do the tests call the code only as its callers do, through its interfaces?
necessary_conditions.why: A test that calls the code as its callers do fails only where a caller would break, so the maintainer can improve a body without fear. Software Engineering at Google calls this [testing through public interfaces](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch12.html).

items.text: For each test, ask whether it reaches anything that a caller can't. If it does, rewrite it to use the interface.
Use the real parts where they run fast and wholly inside the test, and a stand-in only for what's slow or outside it.
Change a body without changing what its interface says, and run the tests. Rewrite each test that fails so that it calls the code through the interface.

necessary_conditions.what: Does breaking any behavior make a test fail?
necessary_conditions.why: A test is worth the faults it catches, so breaking a behavior must make a test fail. Coverage, [mutation testing](https://research.google/pubs/state-of-mutation-testing-at-google/), and [property-based testing](https://hypothesis.works/articles/what-is-property-based-testing/) measure how well the tests catch faults: the lines no test runs, the mutants that survive, and the inputs that a property finds the code fails on.

items.text: Have each test check the result that its case asks for.
Find each line or branch that no test runs, such as by measuring coverage while the tests run, and add a test for each.

Apart from the work, at the time that [the architecture best practice](../architecture/best-practice.md) sets for it, change the code in small ways with a mutation testing tool. For each change under which the tests still pass, first ask whether the part needs the code it changed. Remove the code that no case of the tests calls for, or make it simpler, so that no change of it passes unseen. Where the change can't alter what the code does, mark it with why. Add a test only where the change shows a case that the tests already name and check too loosely, and then report why the design of the test cases missed it, so that whoever designs the cases mends its cause. Add no case there, since a case added to catch a mutant comes from the code that exists, not from what the part must do: a new case goes back to the design.

Apart from the work, at the time that [the architecture best practice](../architecture/best-practice.md) sets for it, run the code over many inputs that the specification allows, such as with property-based tests. For each input that the code fails on, first ask whether the code needs to take it, and narrow what the part takes where it needn't. Else fix the code, keep the input as a fixed test of the case it falls in, and report why the design of the test cases missed it.
Compare each count with the last, and trace a rise to the design of the cases, not to the tests alone.

critical_success_factors.what: Whoever runs the code can fix a wrong input from outside.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the code refuse a wrong input from outside before it acts, with a message from which whoever ran it can fix the input?
necessary_conditions.why: A fault from outside should never leave whoever ran the code stuck or their data half changed. [Fail fast](https://martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/failFast.pdf) checks what comes from outside, such as arguments, files, settings, and the replies of other programs, where it comes in and before the code does anything.

items.text: Where the input comes in, read it into the form that the inside of the code uses, as [parse, don't validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/) says, and check its type, its format, and whether its value makes sense for the task.
Refuse a value that the code can't read, instead of guessing it.
Catch only the errors you mean to handle.
Write the message so that whoever ran the code learns which program refused, what was wrong, where, and what the code accepts.
Write each check so that it runs however someone runs the code, unlike an assert that someone can turn off.
Give the code each wrong input that the specification names. Read each message as the person who ran the code, and check that they can fix the input from the message alone.
